Ibleam
IB-lee-am
proper noun
Hebrew Yible’am, perhaps “he consumes the people,” a town of Manasseh in the plain of Jezreel.

Biblical Definition

Ibleam was a town belonging to the half-tribe of Manasseh, set among the cities of the plain with Beth-shean, Taanach, and Megiddo (Jos 17:11). Like its neighbours, it was a town Manasseh could not, or would not, possess, for neither did Manasseh drive out the inhabitants of Ibleam and her towns, but the Canaanites would dwell in that land (Jdg 1:27). Thus Ibleam belongs to the sad register of the unfinished conquest, the cities suffered to remain in the heart of the inheritance against the plain command of God, who had said, Ye shall make no league with the inhabitants of this land; ye shall throw down their altars (Jdg 2:2). In the days of the kings the town saw a violent end, for it was by the going up to Gur, which is by Ibleam, that Jehu’s men smote Ahaziah king of Judah in his chariot, and he fled to Megiddo and died there (2Ki 9:27). The dictionary marks Ibleam as a town of compromise and of judgment. What Israel failed to cleanse remained a snare, and the plains they would not purge of idolatry became in time the very fields of blood where kings fell under the avenging hand of God.

Webster 1828 Definition

A town of Manasseh in the plain of Jezreel, left unconquered and later a scene of royal bloodshed.

IBLEAM, a town of the half-tribe of Manasseh in the plain of Jezreel.

It is named with Beth-shean, Taanach, and Megiddo among Manasseh’s cities.

Manasseh did not drive out its Canaanite inhabitants.

By the going up to Gur near Ibleam, Ahaziah of Judah was mortally smitten.

It belongs to the register of the unfinished conquest and its judgment.

Key Scripture

Jos 17:11 — "And Manasseh had in Issachar and in Asher Bethshean and her towns, and Ibleam and her towns, and the inhabitants of Dor and her towns, and the inhabitants of Endor and her towns, and the inhabitants of Taanach and her towns, and the inhabitants of Megiddo and her towns, even three countries."

Jdg 1:27 — "Neither did Manasseh drive out the inhabitants of Bethshean and her towns, nor Taanach and her towns, nor the inhabitants of Dor and her towns, nor the inhabitants of Ibleam and her towns, nor the inhabitants of Megiddo and her towns: but the Canaanites would dwell in that land."

2Ki 9:27 — "But when Ahaziah the king of Judah saw this, he fled by the way of the garden house. And Jehu followed after him, and said, Smite him also in the chariot. And they did so at the going up to Gur, which is by Ibleam. And he fled to Megiddo, and died there."

Jdg 2:2 — "And ye shall make no league with the inhabitants of this land; ye shall throw down their altars: but ye have not obeyed my voice: why have ye done this?"

Modern Corruption

A place of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it shows the cost of an unfinished conquest and a league with idolatry.

expand to see more

Ibleam has drawn no redefinition from the present age, surviving as a name in the record of Manasseh’s failure and Ahaziah’s fall. The dictionary records the town that the reader may mark how a spared idolatry returned in time as a field of blood.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the danger of a league with what God commanded to be destroyed. Manasseh suffered the Canaanite to dwell at Ibleam against the voice of the LORD, and the unpurged plain became at last the place where a king was struck down. So the believer is warned that the idols he will not cast out abide to his hurt, and the compromise spared in mercy becomes in time a snare and a sorrow.

Hebrew Roots

From the Hebrew perhaps “he consumes the people,” Ibleam names a town of Manasseh left unconquered.

Ibleam — Hebrew Yible’am, perhaps “he consumes the people.”

It was a town of the half-tribe of Manasseh in the plain of Jezreel.

It is named with Beth-shean, Taanach, and Megiddo.

Manasseh did not drive out its Canaanite inhabitants.

Near it Ahaziah king of Judah was mortally wounded by Jehu’s men.

Usage

"Like Ibleam left unconquered, an idolatry spared returns in time to wound."

"Israel was to make no league with the inhabitants of the land, but throw down their altars."

"The compromise suffered in the heart of the inheritance becomes at last a snare."
